question:
Patient note:
A 54-year-old man presented to the pre-operative clinic this morning for final assessment before an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy scheduled later today for symptomatic cholelithiasis confirmed on ultrasonography. He arrived walking without assistance, reporting that he remains fully active at work as an accountant and exercises three evenings a week on a stationary bicycle; he denies any limitations with climbing two flights of stairs or performing household chores. His surgical history is limited to an appendectomy in adolescence, and he has not undergone any operative procedures, endoscopic interventions, or hospital admissions over the past year. He has never required a plaster cast nor sustained fractures of the hip, pelvis, or long bones, and there has been no recent trauma, stroke, or neurologic injury resulting in weakness or paralysis. He also denies chest pain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or lower-extremity edema, and physical examination confirms normal jugular venous pressure, clear lung fields, and an absence of pedal swelling or dilated superficial veins. Cardiopulmonary review of systems is negative for wheezing or chronic cough, and he reports no history of chronic obstructive lung disease or prior myocardial infarction. Infectious review is unrevealing; he has not experienced fevers, rigors, or productive cough, and he has not required antibiotics or been hospitalized for sepsis or pneumonia in recent weeks. He is a lifelong non-smoker and consumes alcohol socially, averaging one to two beers on weekends. Review of hematologic history is notable in that, during a routine evaluation five years ago for an incidentally prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time, he was found to harbor an antiphospholipid antibody consistent with a lupus anticoagulant pattern on confirmatory mixing studies. He has never had a leg clot, pulmonary embolus, spontaneous abortion, or other clinical thrombotic event, and he has not been treated with chronic anticoagulation, but the result has remained persistently positive on repeat testing. There is no family record of venous or arterial thrombosis, and neither parent nor his two siblings have been diagnosed with thrombophilia. He has not been exposed to unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin in the past, and there is no concern for drug-induced platelet abnormalities. Past medical history is otherwise significant for a stage II left-sided colon carcinoma resected laparoscopically two years ago; margins were negative and he received six months of adjuvant capecitabine, after which surveillance colonoscopy and serial carcinoembryonic antigen levels have remained reassuringly normal, though he continues to follow with oncology every six months. He has no diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease. Medications include atorvastatin 20 mg nightly for hyperlipidemia and a daily multivitamin; he takes no hormonal therapy, corticosteroids, or erythropoietin. Vital signs today show blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. Body mass index is 27 kg/m². Laboratory studies obtained yesterday revealed hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, platelet count 238 × 10⁹/L, normal renal and hepatic panels, and a slightly prolonged aPTT consistent with his known antibody; international normalized ratio, prothrombin time, and fibrinogen are within reference ranges. He arrives with peripheral intravenous access only, and no central venous catheter is in place. Physical examination shows a well-nourished male in no distress, with clear oropharynx, supple neck, regular heart rhythm without murmurs, lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally, a soft non-tender abdomen with palpable gallbladder edge on deep inspiration, and intact distal pulses. Skin inspection reveals no discoloration or ulcerations of the lower extremities, and there is no calf tenderness. Neurologic exam is non-focal. He confirms adherence to pre-operative fasting guidelines and has withheld his morning statin as instructed. The anesthesiology team has performed an airway assessment and anticipates an uncomplicated endotracheal intubation. Consent has been obtained after discussing the minimally invasive nature of the planned four-port laparoscopic approach, anticipated one-hour operating time, and expected overnight observation. No prophylactic anticoagulant has yet been administered pending completion of risk stratification.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini venous thromboembolism score adds weighted perioperative risk factors:
- Age 41–60 years: age 54 → 1 point.
- BMI >25 kg/m²: BMI 27 → 1 point.
- Laparoscopic surgery lasting >45 minutes: planned duration 60 minutes → 2 points. Count the operation once.
- Current or previous malignancy: resected colon cancer qualifies despite remission → 2 points.
- Documented thrombophilia: persistently positive lupus anticoagulant qualifies even without prior thrombosis → 3 points.
- No additional documented factors: he is ambulatory and has no prior VTE, family history of VTE, central line, or recent immobilization → 0 points.
Sum: 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 0 = 9.
Final answer: 9
